scope: AQA Chemistry school mock: AS atomic structure and taught A2 aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, ester hydrolysis, acylation, Kp, pH/Kw/Ka and Arrhenius. No buffer, chromatography/NMR, untaught A2 or laboratory procedures.
notes: Eight wholly original theory and calculation problems; not copies of AQA papers or official mark schemes. Marking is provisional, supports manual correction, and does not instruct any handling of chemicals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Assign unknown carbonyls from oxidation-test results
questions.prompt: Two labelled pure samples X and Y are known to be either an aldehyde or a ketone. In reported tests, X gives a silver deposit with Tollens' reagent and a brick-red solid with Fehling's solution; Y shows neither change. No experiment is required for this question. (a) Identify each functional group. (b) Name the metal-containing species observed and describe the corresponding redox changes. (c) Explain why Y does not give these mild oxidation-test results. (d) State the type of alcohol formed when each sample is reduced by a suitable reducing agent. [8 marks]
markPoints: Sample X is an aldehyde because it gives positive results with both oxidation tests.
Sample Y is a ketone, given that it is known to be one of the two carbonyl classes and shows no positive test.
In Tollens' test Ag⁺ is reduced to metallic silver, Ag, producing the silver deposit.
The aldehyde functional group in X is oxidised (ultimately to a carboxylic acid/carboxylate form).
Fehling's positive result is a brick-red copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, solid.
In Fehling's test copper(II) is reduced to copper(I).
Ordinary ketones are not readily oxidised by these mild oxidising tests, explaining Y's negative results.
Reduction of an aldehyde forms a primary alcohol whereas reduction of a ketone forms a secondary alcohol.
questions.modelAnswer: Sample X is an aldehyde because it gives positive results with both oxidation tests. Sample Y is a ketone, given that it is known to be one of the two carbonyl classes and shows no positive test. In Tollens' test Ag⁺ is reduced to metallic silver, Ag, producing the silver deposit. The aldehyde functional group in X is oxidised (ultimately to a carboxylic acid/carboxylate form). Fehling's positive result is a brick-red copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O, solid. In Fehling's test copper(II) is reduced to copper(I). Ordinary ketones are not readily oxidised by these mild oxidising tests, explaining Y's negative results. Reduction of an aldehyde forms a primary alcohol whereas reduction of a ketone forms a secondary alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Predict soap and glycerol amounts from a triglyceride
questions.subtopic: Triglyceride hydrolysis: soap, glycerol and yield
questions.prompt: In a theoretical mass-balance problem, 1.77 g of a triglyceride has a relative molecular mass of 885. Its complete alkaline hydrolysis yields one molecule of glycerol and three molecules of a long-chain carboxylate salt (soap) per triglyceride molecule. The relative formula mass of the salt is 304. A recovered soap sample has mass 1.50 g. (a) Determine the amount of triglyceride. (b) Calculate the theoretical amount and maximum mass of soap. (c) Calculate the percentage yield. (d) State how soap differs chemically from biodiesel. [8 marks]
markPoints: Amount of triglyceride = 1.77/885 = 0.00200 mol.
A triglyceride contains three ester links and yields three carboxylate ions/salts when hydrolysed under alkaline conditions.
One molecule of glycerol is released per triglyceride molecule, so theoretical glycerol amount is 0.00200 mol.
The theoretical amount of soap is 3 × 0.00200 = 0.00600 mol.
The theoretical maximum mass of soap is 0.00600 × 304 = 1.824 g.
Percentage yield = 1.50/1.824 × 100.
Percentage yield is about 82.2%.
Soap is a salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid; biodiesel is a mixture of methyl esters of long-chain carboxylic acids.
questions.modelAnswer: Amount of triglyceride = 1.77/885 = 0.00200 mol. A triglyceride contains three ester links and yields three carboxylate ions/salts when hydrolysed under alkaline conditions. One molecule of glycerol is released per triglyceride molecule, so theoretical glycerol amount is 0.00200 mol. The theoretical amount of soap is 3 × 0.00200 = 0.00600 mol. The theoretical maximum mass of soap is 0.00600 × 304 = 1.824 g. Percentage yield = 1.50/1.824 × 100. Percentage yield is about 82.2%. Soap is a salt of a long-chain carboxylic acid; biodiesel is a mixture of methyl esters of long-chain carboxylic acids.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Compare acylation products of an amine and an anhydride
questions.subtopic: Identify acylation products and industrial comparison
questions.prompt: Consider only these written reaction schemes, not laboratory preparation. Scheme I: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → an organic product + HCl. Scheme II: (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O → carboxylic acid products. (a) Name the organic product of Scheme I and give its functional group. (b) Identify the general reaction mechanism of an acyl chloride with a primary amine, and why its carbonyl carbon is attacked. (c) Give the organic products of Scheme II. (d) Give one industrial reason ethanoic anhydride may be preferred over ethanoyl chloride. [7 marks]
markPoints: The acyl group CH₃CO– becomes bonded to the nitrogen-containing group from methylamine.
The Scheme I organic product is N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃.
The organic functional group is an amide.
Acyl chlorides react with primary amines by nucleophilic addition–elimination.
The carbonyl C is electrophilic (δ+) because the polar C=O bond draws electron density towards O.
Ethanoic anhydride reacts with water to give two equivalents of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH.
Anhydride processes avoid producing corrosive hydrogen chloride as the by-product, unlike ethanoyl chloride; the acid by-product is easier to handle.
questions.modelAnswer: The acyl group CH₃CO– becomes bonded to the nitrogen-containing group from methylamine. The Scheme I organic product is N-methylethanamide, CH₃CONHCH₃. The organic functional group is an amide. Acyl chlorides react with primary amines by nucleophilic addition–elimination. The carbonyl C is electrophilic (δ+) because the polar C=O bond draws electron density towards O. Ethanoic anhydride reacts with water to give two equivalents of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH. Anhydride processes avoid producing corrosive hydrogen chloride as the by-product, unlike ethanoyl chloride; the acid by-product is easier to handle.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Weak monoprotic acid pH and percentage dissociation
questions.subtopic: Weak acid Ka and approximation validity
questions.prompt: A hypothetical weak monoprotic acid HA has initial concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³ and Ka = 1.80 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ at 298 K. Assume no other significant source of H⁺. (a) Write the Ka expression. (b) State the weak-acid approximation. (c) Calculate the equilibrium [H⁺] and pH using that approximation. (d) Calculate the percentage of acid dissociated and decide whether the approximation is appropriate. (e) Compare the pH with a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ fully dissociated monoprotic strong acid. [8 marks]
markPoints: For weak dissociation, assume [HA] at equilibrium ≈ initial concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³.
Assuming [H⁺] ≈ [A⁻] = x, the expression becomes Ka ≈ x²/0.100.
Percentage dissociation = (1.34 × 10⁻³/0.100) × 100 ≈ 1.34%.
The approximately 1.34% dissociation is small, supporting the [HA] ≈ 0.100 approximation.
A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ fully dissociated monoprotic strong acid has pH ≈ 1.00, lower than the weak acid's pH.
questions.modelAnswer: Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. For weak dissociation, assume [HA] at equilibrium ≈ initial concentration 0.100 mol dm⁻³. Assuming [H⁺] ≈ [A⁻] = x, the expression becomes Ka ≈ x²/0.100. [H⁺] ≈ √(1.80 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.100) = 1.34 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. pH = −log₁₀(1.34 × 10⁻³) ≈ 2.87. Percentage dissociation = (1.34 × 10⁻³/0.100) × 100 ≈ 1.34%. The approximately 1.34% dissociation is small, supporting the [HA] ≈ 0.100 approximation. A 0.100 mol dm⁻³ fully dissociated monoprotic strong acid has pH ≈ 1.00, lower than the weak acid's pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Calculate strong-base pH with a doubled hydroxide concentration
questions.subtopic: Kw and complete dissociation of strong hydroxide
questions.prompt: At 298 K, Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. A theoretical solution contains 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, and is assumed fully dissociated. (a) Determine the hydroxide-ion concentration. (b) Determine hydrogen-ion concentration using Kw. (c) Calculate pOH and pH. (d) Explain why using 0.0150 mol dm⁻³ directly as [OH⁻] would be wrong. [7 marks]
markPoints: Full dissociation of Ca(OH)₂ produces two moles of OH⁻ per mole of formula units.
Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻], so [H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻].
Using 0.0150 as [OH⁻] neglects the 2:1 hydroxide-to-calcium-hydroxide stoichiometry.
questions.modelAnswer: Full dissociation of Ca(OH)₂ produces two moles of OH⁻ per mole of formula units. [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.0150 = 0.0300 mol dm⁻³. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻], so [H⁺] = Kw/[OH⁻]. [H⁺] = (1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴)/0.0300 = 3.33 × 10⁻¹³ mol dm⁻³. pOH = −log₁₀(0.0300) ≈ 1.523. pH = 14.000 − pOH = 12.477 (or −log₁₀[H⁺]). Using 0.0150 as [OH⁻] neglects the 2:1 hydroxide-to-calcium-hydroxide stoichiometry.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Kp and pressure response for sulfur oxide equilibrium
questions.subtopic: Equilibrium mole fractions with net gaseous mole change
questions.prompt: For the idealised gaseous equilibrium 2SO₃(g) ⇌ 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g), initially 1.00 mol SO₃ is present with none of the products. At equilibrium, 0.600 mol SO₃ has reacted. Total equilibrium pressure is 130 kPa and temperature is constant. (a) Find equilibrium amounts and mole fractions of all gases. (b) Find each partial pressure. (c) Write and evaluate Kp, including its units. (d) Predict the equilibrium response to a pressure increase at fixed temperature and state whether Kp changes. [8 marks]
markPoints: Equilibrium amounts are SO₃ = 0.400 mol, SO₂ = 0.600 mol and O₂ = 0.300 mol.
Total moles at equilibrium = 0.400 + 0.600 + 0.300 = 1.300 mol.
Mole fractions of SO₃, SO₂ and O₂ are 0.400/1.300, 0.600/1.300 and 0.300/1.300.
Partial pressures are p(SO₃) = 40.0 kPa, p(SO₂) = 60.0 kPa and p(O₂) = 30.0 kPa.
Kp = p(SO₂)² × p(O₂) / p(SO₃)².
Substitution gives Kp = (60.0² × 30.0)/(40.0²) = 67.5.
Kp units are kPa because the overall partial-pressure power is (2 + 1 − 2) = +1.
Increasing pressure favours fewer gas molecules, shifting left towards SO₃, while Kp remains unchanged at constant temperature.
questions.modelAnswer: Equilibrium amounts are SO₃ = 0.400 mol, SO₂ = 0.600 mol and O₂ = 0.300 mol. Total moles at equilibrium = 0.400 + 0.600 + 0.300 = 1.300 mol. Mole fractions of SO₃, SO₂ and O₂ are 0.400/1.300, 0.600/1.300 and 0.300/1.300. Partial pressures are p(SO₃) = 40.0 kPa, p(SO₂) = 60.0 kPa and p(O₂) = 30.0 kPa. Kp = p(SO₂)² × p(O₂) / p(SO₃)². Substitution gives Kp = (60.0² × 30.0)/(40.0²) = 67.5. Kp units are kPa because the overall partial-pressure power is (2 + 1 − 2) = +1. Increasing pressure favours fewer gas molecules, shifting left towards SO₃, while Kp remains unchanged at constant temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Activation energy from two Arrhenius-plot points
questions.prompt: For a hypothetical reaction, a graph of ln k (vertical axis) against 1/T (horizontal axis, units K⁻¹) is linear. Two points on its best-fit line are (0.00320 K⁻¹, −3.10) and (0.00300 K⁻¹, −1.10). The gas constant R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate the line gradient. (b) Determine the activation energy in kJ mol⁻¹. (c) Calculate the y-intercept ln A and state what A means in the Arrhenius equation. (d) Explain what happens to the reaction's activation energy when an appropriate catalyst is used and what does not change about its enthalpy change. [7 marks]
markPoints: Arrhenius form ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT) gives gradient = −Ea/R.
Ea = −gradient × R = 10 000 × 8.31 = 83 100 J mol⁻¹.
Ea = 83.1 kJ mol⁻¹.
A is the Arrhenius pre-exponential (frequency) factor; A ≈ e²⁸·⁹ ≈ 3.56 × 10¹² in the corresponding units of k.
A catalyst supplies a lower-activation-energy route but does not change the reaction enthalpy ΔH.
questions.modelAnswer: Gradient = (−1.10 − (−3.10))/(0.00300 − 0.00320) = −10 000 K. Arrhenius form ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT) gives gradient = −Ea/R. Ea = −gradient × R = 10 000 × 8.31 = 83 100 J mol⁻¹. Ea = 83.1 kJ mol⁻¹. Intercept ln A = −3.10 − (−10 000 × 0.00320) = 28.9. A is the Arrhenius pre-exponential (frequency) factor; A ≈ e²⁸·⁹ ≈ 3.56 × 10¹² in the corresponding units of k. A catalyst supplies a lower-activation-energy route but does not change the reaction enthalpy ΔH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Interpret two isotopes in an elemental mass spectrum
questions.subtopic: Mononuclear isotope masses, relative abundances and ion charges
questions.prompt: The mass spectrum of an element E has two peaks from singly charged mononuclear isotope ions at m/z 63 and 65. Their relative peak intensities are 69.2 and 30.8, respectively. (a) Explain why there are two peaks for the same element. (b) State the relative abundances and calculate relative atomic mass. (c) If a small proportion of each isotope forms a 2+ mononuclear ion rather than a 1+ ion, predict the two new m/z values and explain why. [7 marks]
markPoints: The two peaks represent isotopes with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
For singly charged mononuclear ions, m/z values are approximately the isotope masses 63 and 65.
The relative abundances are 69.2% and 30.8%, or fractions 0.692 and 0.308.
Weighted calculation Ar = (63 × 0.692) + (65 × 0.308).
Relative atomic mass Ar = 63.616, approximately 63.6.
The doubly charged mass-63 mononuclear ion gives m/z = 63/2 = 31.5.
The doubly charged mass-65 mononuclear ion gives m/z = 65/2 = 32.5 because mass-to-charge ratio halves when charge doubles.
questions.modelAnswer: The two peaks represent isotopes with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. For singly charged mononuclear ions, m/z values are approximately the isotope masses 63 and 65. The relative abundances are 69.2% and 30.8%, or fractions 0.692 and 0.308. Weighted calculation Ar = (63 × 0.692) + (65 × 0.308). Relative atomic mass Ar = 63.616, approximately 63.6. The doubly charged mass-63 mononuclear ion gives m/z = 63/2 = 31.5. The doubly charged mass-65 mononuclear ion gives m/z = 65/2 = 32.5 because mass-to-charge ratio halves when charge doubles.
